newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch closing debt market report.
newsitem.headline: Dutch closing debt market report.

text.p: Dutch bonds ended well above the session's low on Monday, tracking the German Bund future upward in quiet trade in the afternoon.
Dealers said throughout a thinly traded day most attention was focused on futures, resulting in a deserted cash market.
"People just won't invest ahead of FOMC," one dealer said.
The U.S. central bank's Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meets on Tuesday to consider monetary policy.
Recent inflationary pressures and comments of Federal Reserve Bank chairman Alan Greenspan have led the market to factor in a 0.25 percent hike in the federal fund target.
"If they don't move, there'll be a reaction in the market, if they hike 25 basis points, there won't," one dealer said.
Another said the move in U.S. interest rates as such would be of little importance as it had already been priced in.
"What counts is their explanation of the move," he said.
Some dealers said the sharp drop in Italian bonds had caused some pressure in the German and consequently in the Dutch bond markets at midsession, but they were divided over the grounds.
"At Liffe, the Italian pit is right next to the German one, and although fundamentally, there's no link, the sentiment easily jumps over from one to another," one said.
Another said dealers who had got overloaded with Italian bonds which they could not get rid of, might have started to short-sell German bunds to hedge themselves.
"The obvious move -- out of Italian into German bonds -- did not occur. EMU-uncertainty causes market players not to opt for Bunds that easily," he said.
The direction of the market was unclear, dealers said.

"The old A-B-C seems gone, making the market hard to handle," one dealer said. "Normally, a trader who has an opinion running beyond fifteen minutes or so, is considered a seer. These matters are much too long term for many of us," he said.
